idiom_name: capability negotiation: one query operation returning a handle or an explicit negative
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: give the queried object one uniform question - 'do you support capability X?' - that returns either a usable handle (pointer, reference, interface value, capability object) or an explicit negative (null/None/nil/false/error), and make every caller branch on that answer instead of on the object's type. Keep each capability a narrow interface of its own, keep the answer set stable for the object's lifetime (reflexive, symmetric and transitive wherever the runtime allows, which is what COM demands of QueryInterface), and document the lifetime and ownership of the returned handle. Reserve the runtime query for genuinely dynamic boundaries; wherever the capability set is known statically, a base interface, generic bound or sealed variant is preferable.
pitfalls: Returning yes with a handle that fails on the first capability call -> the positive answer gives no safe negotiation fallback -> make support imply a callable contract and validate the returned handle before publication.

Letting the answer change for the same object -> cached handles become stale and callers observe time-dependent support -> keep the interface set stable for the object lifetime or expose an explicit refresh/version contract.
Using the query as authorization -> ACL state makes support nondeterministic and cached pointers can bypass checks -> authorize possession and use of the returned handle separately.
Using respond_to?/hasattr as a signature check -> a name-only positive result still leads to wrong-arity or wrong-type calls -> use a typed protocol or validate the call boundary.

Forwarding an aggregated object's interfaces with a different pointer per query -> COM-style symmetry, transitivity and identity break -> return stable interface views and honor the wrapper's unwrapping contract.
Advertising a capability from a construction-time flag that later changes -> cached decisions drift from runtime behavior -> version the negotiation or keep the capability set immutable.
Adding every optional operation to one fat interface -> legacy implementers return false or throw and unrelated clients recompile -> split cohesive interfaces and query only the one needed.

Treating a versioned numeric flag as a complete capability contract -> peers can agree on a bit while disagreeing on signature or lifetime -> pair versioned identifiers with typed handles and an explicit unknown-capability fallback.

Querying a decorator without preserving its underlying capabilities -> wrappers make supported operations appear absent and force unnecessary fallback -> forward the capability query or provide an explicit Unwrap contract.

Cascading dynamic_cast/else-if tests down a closed, known variant set -> the chain is a disguised type switch that silently mis-handles new subclasses and must be edited at every rung -> match exhaustively over a sealed hierarchy or promote the operation to the base interface, and reserve queries for cross-casts to genuinely optional interfaces.

Inferring platform support from a User-Agent or brand string instead of probing the feature -> spoofed and fragmented UA strings take the wrong branch exactly where a feature test would have succeeded -> test the feature itself ('geolocation' in navigator) and fall back to a polyfill on absence.

Relying on dynamic_cast at a plugin boundary where RTTI is disabled or the cast crosses a dynamic library -> the query compiles but fails or aborts only in production builds -> use a facility specified to work across that boundary (COM QueryInterface, Qt's qobject_cast, LLVM's isa/dyn_cast).
